title: C-Strings and char* Pointers - Title Slide
summary: Title slide for Unit 2d covering C-Strings and char* pointers in C++, taught by Mark Redekopp as part of CS 103.
main_text: This unit covers C-Strings and char* pointers in C/C++. C-Strings are character arrays that represent text data in C and C++. The char* type is a pointer to a character, commonly used to reference C-strings. This unit explores the relationship between character arrays, pointers, and string manipulation functions available in the cstring library.
notes_text: This is a foundational topic for understanding how strings work at a low level in C/C++, before the convenience of the C++ string class.

title: The NULL Pointer - Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing the concept of the NULL pointer (NULL or nullptr) in C/C++.
main_text: This section introduces the NULL pointer concept. NULL or nullptr is a special pointer value used in C and C++ to indicate that a pointer does not point to any valid memory address. Understanding the NULL pointer is essential before working with C-strings, as many C-string library functions return NULL to indicate failure or absence of a match.
notes_text: The NULL pointer is a prerequisite concept for understanding how C-string functions like strchr and strstr signal that a character or substring was not found.

title: Motivation for the NULL Pointer - Problem Setup
summary: Demonstrates the need for NULL pointers using a function that returns a pointer to the first negative integer in an array, showing what goes wrong when no negative exists.
main_text: Suppose you write a function to return a pointer to the first negative integer in an array and then use that pointer to make the value positive. The function signature is: int* firstNeg(int dat[], int len). The implementation iterates through the array, and if dat[i] < 0, it returns &dat[i]. The code after the loop is highlighted as problematic: what happens if no negative number is found? The function has no return statement for that case. In the example, int dat1[5] = {14, 8, -3, 2, -9}, and int* ptr1 = firstNeg(dat1, 5) returns a pointer to dat[2] which holds -3. Then *ptr1 = -*ptr1 makes it positive. But the question is: what might go wrong if the array has no negative numbers?
notes_text: This motivates the need for a sentinel return value. Without a way to signal 'not found,' the caller would dereference an undefined pointer, leading to undefined behavior or a crash. The memory diagram shows dat1 at addresses 73a0-73b0 with values 14, 8, -3, 2, -9, and the function returning a pointer to address 73a8 (dat[2]).

images.description: Memory diagram showing an integer array dat1 at addresses 73a0 through 73b0 with values 14, 8, -3, 2, -9 stored in dat[0] through dat[4], with the int* return pointing to address 73a8 (the first negative value -3)

title: Motivation for the NULL Pointer - The Problem Case
summary: Shows what happens when calling firstNeg on an array with no negative numbers, highlighting the need for a special invalid pointer value.
main_text: Continuing the firstNeg example, what should the function return if there are NO negative numbers in the array? The function body now shows 'return ??;' highlighted, indicating the missing return case. A second array int dat2[5] = {14, 8, 5, 2, 9} has all positive values. When int* ptr2 = firstNeg(dat2, 5) is called, the function cannot find a negative number. Then *ptr2 = -*ptr2 would try to dereference an invalid pointer, causing undefined behavior. It would be nice if there was some address/pointer value we could use to signify 'INVALID' or 'Bad Address'. This motivates the introduction of NULL.
notes_text: The memory diagram on the right shows dat2 at addresses 73a0-73b0 with all positive values (14, 8, 3, 2, 9), and the int* return is marked with '??' indicating no valid address can be returned. The key insight is that no valid array element address can serve as a sentinel, so a dedicated invalid value is needed.

images.description: Memory diagram showing array dat2 at addresses 73a0-73b0 with all positive values (14, 8, 3, 2, 9) and the int* return marked with '??' to indicate no valid return address exists

title: Motivation for the NULL Pointer - The Solution
summary: Introduces NULL as the solution for signaling an invalid pointer return, demonstrating how to check for NULL before dereferencing.
main_text: The solution to the problem is to return NULL when no negative number is found. The function now has 'return NULL;' at the end. In main, after calling firstNeg on an array with no negatives (dat2[5] = {14, 8, 5, 2, 9}), the code checks: if(ptr != NULL) { cout << "Num: " << -*ptr2 << endl; } else { cout << "None" << endl; }. This demonstrates the pattern: always check if a pointer is NULL before dereferencing it. NULL (or nullptr) represents address 0, which is reserved as an invalid address that no real data will ever occupy.
notes_text: The memory diagram shows dat2 with all positive values. The key pattern introduced here is the NULL check before dereference, which is fundamental to safe pointer usage in C/C++. This same pattern is used extensively with C-string functions like strchr and strstr.

images.description: Memory diagram showing array dat2 at addresses 73a0-73b0 with values 14, 8, 3, 2, 9, with the int* return marked with '??' since no negative exists

title: NULL and nullptr Explained
summary: Explains that C/C++ chose address 0 as the INVALID pointer, defines NULL and nullptr keywords, and describes proper usage patterns.
main_text: Strange question: Is there a building at 3715 McClintock Ave.? There is no way to really tell just from the address whether it is valid or whether good data resides there. Nothing about a memory address (e.g. 0x7fffecb0) would tell us whether good data resides there. So C/C++ chose address 0 to mean INVALID POINTER and defined the keyword NULL (in <cstdlib>) or now nullptr (in C++11) as address 0. NULL or nullptr are literally replaced with 0. To use nullptr, compile with the C++11 version: g++ -std=c++11 -g -o test test.cpp. You should NEVER dereference a null pointer (it will likely cause a crash). Use NULL or nullptr to: (1) Initialize a pointer variable when you do not know what it should point to yet, e.g. int* p = NULL; (2) As a return value when a function cannot return a pointer to good data; (3) Check for bad pointers, e.g. int* p = firstNeg(...); if(p != nullptr) { /* safe to use p */ } or equivalently if(p).
notes_text: NULL and nullptr are substitutes for address 0. They should be used to indicate an INVALID pointer because nothing good ever lives at address 0. This is similar to the null character ('\0') but the null character is a char type while NULL/nullptr are pointer types. The analogy to a street address helps: knowing an address does not guarantee something valid exists there.

title: Other Uses of NULL - strchr and strstr
summary: Introduces strchr and strstr from the cstring library as functions that return pointers and use NULL to indicate a character or substring was not found.
main_text: Another example from the <cstring> library is strchr or strstr, which returns a pointer to the first occurrence of a character or another C-String in a source C-string. The function signatures are: char *strchr(char *src, char c); and char *strstr(char *src, char* target);. The key question raised is: what should be returned if the character does not occur in the string? The answer is NULL, following the same pattern established with the firstNeg example.
notes_text: strchr returns a pointer to the first occurrence of character c in the string src, or NULL if not found. strstr returns a pointer to the first occurrence of the substring target in src, or NULL if not found. Both require the caller to check for NULL before using the returned pointer.

title: NULL Summary
summary: Summarizes that NULL and nullptr equal 0, are used for invalid addresses, and must be checked before dereferencing any pointer.
main_text: NULL and nullptr both evaluate to 0. They are used to indicate an INVALID address. Before dereferencing a pointer, always check that it is NOT NULL using: if(ptr != NULL) { /* safe to dereference */ }. The slide shows three pointer variables of different types (int* ptr1, char* word, double* ptr2) all initialized to 0 (NULL), visually reinforcing that NULL applies to all pointer types regardless of what they point to.
notes_text: This is a critical safety rule in C/C++ programming. Any pointer that might be NULL must be checked before dereferencing. Dereferencing a NULL pointer causes undefined behavior, typically a segmentation fault crash. The visual shows that NULL is type-agnostic: it works with int*, char*, double*, or any other pointer type.

images.description: Three pointer variables (int* ptr1, char* word, double* ptr2) each shown as a box containing the value 0, illustrating that NULL applies to all pointer types

title: Caution: NULL (or nullptr) != '\0'
summary: Clarifies the critical distinction between NULL/nullptr (pointer type for invalid addresses) and '\0' (char type for end of string), noting both have value 0 but different types.
main_text: NULL or nullptr are pointer types, used to indicate an INVALID pointer. The null character '\0' is a char type used in character strings to indicate the end of a string. Both have the same value (0) but are different types. This distinction is important: NULL/nullptr is a pointer concept (address 0, meaning 'points to nothing valid'), while '\0' is a character concept (the character with ASCII value 0, used as a string terminator). Confusing the two is a common source of errors for students learning C/C++.
notes_text: This is one of the most frequently confused concepts in C/C++. NULL is used in pointer comparisons (if ptr == NULL), while '\0' is used in character comparisons (if str[i] == '\0'). They are semantically different even though both evaluate to 0. The compiler distinguishes them by type context.

title: Revisiting C-Strings (Character Arrays) - Section Divider
summary: Section divider transitioning to a deeper exploration of C-Strings as character arrays and their relationship with char* pointers.
main_text: This section revisits C-Strings, which are character arrays in C/C++. Having established the concept of NULL pointers, the lecture now dives deeper into how C-Strings work with pointers, how cin and cout handle char* types differently from other pointer types, and the concept of const char* for string constants.
notes_text: This section builds on prior knowledge of character arrays and null-terminated strings from earlier units, now incorporating pointer concepts to provide a more complete understanding.

title: cout and char* - Special Behavior
summary: Explains that cout treats char* pointers differently from other pointer types, printing the entire string rather than the address value.
main_text: cin/cout determine everything they do based on the type of data passed. But cin/cout have a unique/special relationship with char* types. Generally, when cout is given a variable or expression of any type, it will print the value stored in that exact variable. Exception: when cout is given a char*, it will assume it is pointing at a C-string, go to that address, and loop through each character, printing them out. Example code demonstrates: cout << x prints 5 (the int value), cout << dat prints 400 (the address, since dat is int*), but cout << word prints 'Hello' (the string content, since word is char*). Also cout << name prints 'Hello' (name is char* pointing to word). cout << word+3 prints 'lo' (starting from index 3). cout << name+1 prints 'ello'. To print the actual address of a char*, cast it: cout << (int*) name prints 440 (the address).
notes_text: The memory diagram shows int x = 5 at some address, dat = 400 pointing to an int array of zeros, and word = 470 pointing to a char array containing 'H','e','l','l','o','\0'. char* name = word makes name also point to address 470. The key takeaway is that cout << char_ptr prints the string, not the address. To get the address, cast to (int*) or (void*).

images.description: Memory diagram showing int x with value 5, int* dat pointing to address 400 with zeros, and char* word/name pointing to address 470 containing 'Hello\0'

title: cin and char* - Special Behavior
summary: Explains that cin treats char* pointers specially by writing input characters into the memory location the pointer references, assuming it points to a character array.
main_text: cin/cout determine everything they do based on the type of data passed. But cin/cout have a unique/special relationship with char* types. When cin is given a variable, it will store the input data in that exact variable. Exception: when cin is given a char*, it will assume it is pointing at a C-string, go to that address, and place the typed characters in that memory. Example: cin >> dat does not work for int* (you need a loop), but cin >> name stores many characters starting at address 470 (where name points). This means cin will write characters directly into the memory that the char* points to, so you must ensure the pointer points to a valid, sufficiently large character array.
notes_text: The memory layout is the same as the previous slide. The critical point is that cin >> char_ptr writes to the memory the pointer references. If the pointer does not point to allocated memory, or if the input is longer than the allocated space, this causes buffer overflow and undefined behavior. Always ensure your char* points to a large enough array before using cin.

images.description: Memory diagram showing int x with value 5, int* dat pointing to address 400 with zeros, and char* word/name pointing to address 470 containing 'Hello\0'

title: 2 Types, 2 Actions - char vs char*
summary: Summarizes how cout handles char (prints ASCII character) versus char* (loops and prints entire string until null character).
main_text: In this class, it will be helpful to 'just know' how cout handles a char and char*. When cout receives a char, it prints the ASCII character corresponding to that value. When cout receives a char*, it loops and prints the entire string, character by character, until it finds the null character ('\0'). This distinction is fundamental: char is a single character value, while char* is a pointer to the beginning of a null-terminated string. The behavior of cout changes entirely based on which type it receives.
notes_text: This is a concise rule students should memorize. The same distinction applies to cin: cin >> char_variable reads one character, while cin >> char_ptr reads a word (sequence of characters until whitespace) into the array the pointer references.

title: 2 Types, 2 Actions - Example
summary: Concrete example showing cout << word[0] prints 'H' (single char) while cout << word prints 'Hello' (entire string via char*).
main_text: Given: char word[10] = "Hello"; char *name = word; The example demonstrates: cout << word[0] << endl; -- Here word[0] is a char, so cout prints 'H' (the single ASCII character). cout << word << endl; -- Here word is a char* (array decays to pointer), so cout loops through memory starting at address 470 and prints 'Hello' (all characters until it reaches the null terminator '\0'). The memory diagram shows char* name holding address 470, and at address 470 the characters H, e, l, l, o, \0 are stored.
notes_text: This is the practical demonstration of the rule from the previous slide. The terminal output boxes show 'H' for the char case and 'Hello' for the char* case. Understanding this distinction is critical for debugging output issues in C/C++ programs.

images.description: Memory diagram showing char* name at address 460 holding value 470, and at address 470 the character array word containing 'H','e','l','l','o','\0', with terminal output boxes showing 'H' for word[0] and 'Hello' for word

title: C-String Constants and const char*
summary: Explains that string literals in quotes are stored as anonymous const character arrays in memory, and their type is const char*.
main_text: C-String constants are the things we type in double quotes (e.g., "Hello") and are stored somewhere in memory chosen by the compiler as anonymous const character arrays. For example, as if: const anonymous-str1[6] = "Hello"; and const anonymous-str2[5] = "Bye!";. When you write a string constant like "Hello", the computer gives back the starting address of the anonymous array, and its type is const char*. A char* is the type because an array is ALWAYS known by its starting address. The const qualifier is there because you cannot and should not change the contents of a string constant. When passing a C-string constant to a function, the parameter type should be const char*. C/C++ considers the type of a string constant (e.g., "Hi") to be const char*. Example code shows strcpy(name, "Tommy") where "Tommy" is stored at address 300 and copied into the name array at address 240.
notes_text: The memory diagram shows: at address 800, 'Hello\0' is stored; at address 740, 'Bye!\0' is stored; const char* pointers at 740 and 744 reference these. The strcpy call copies from address 300 (where 'Tommy\0' lives) into name at address 240. This illustrates that string literals have a real memory location and a pointer to that location is what gets passed around.

images.description: Memory diagram showing string constants 'Hello\0' at address 800 and 'Bye!\0' at address 740, with const char* pointers referencing them, and strcpy copying 'Tommy' from address 300 to name array at address 240

title: Constant Strings are const char* - Code Example
summary: Code example demonstrating operations on string constants, pointer arithmetic with string literals, and the relationship between constant strings and const char*.
main_text: A complete code example explores constant strings: cout << "Hello" prints 'Hello' (cout receives the const char* address 470 and prints the string). cout << *"Bye" prints 'B' (dereferencing the pointer gives the first character). cout << *("Bye")+1 prints 'y' (the character at index 1, equivalent to ("Bye")[1]). cout << "Hello"+1 prints 'ello' (pointer arithmetic: starting from the second character). The code also references strcat("Good", "bye") which would fail because strcat requires the first argument to be a modifiable char array with enough space, and "Good" is a const char* pointing to read-only memory. The memory diagram shows 'Hello\0' stored at address 470 and 'Bye\0' at address 520.
notes_text: This example reinforces that string literals are const char* pointers and can be used with pointer arithmetic and dereferencing. The strcat example in comments illustrates a common error: trying to modify a string constant. The prototype reminder shows char* strcat(char* destination, const char* source), making it clear the destination must be modifiable.

images.description: Memory boxes showing 'Hello\0' stored at address 470 and 'Bye\0' stored at address 520

title: Owning Your Memory - Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing the concept of memory ownership, distinguishing between knowing an address and owning the memory at that address.
main_text: This section introduces a critical concept in C/C++ programming: owning the memory that a pointer references. A pointer stores an address, but having an address does not mean you own or can write to the memory at that address. Understanding memory ownership is essential for avoiding segmentation faults and undefined behavior when working with char* pointers and C-strings.
notes_text: Memory ownership is a fundamental concept that distinguishes safe from unsafe pointer usage. This section prepares students to understand why they must allocate arrays before using char* pointers to write data.

title: Knowing vs. Owning an Address
summary: Uses a real-world moving analogy to explain the difference between knowing a memory address and owning the memory at that address.
main_text: Scenario: You are moving. The movers ask: 'What is the address of your new place where we should put all this stuff?' You answer: '1600 Pennsylvania Ave.' What will happen when they go to that address and try to put your stuff there? Obviously, you do not own the White House at 1600 Pennsylvania Ave, so this would not work. KNOWING an address vs. OWNING the property at that address are VERY DIFFERENT. Similarly, when we have a pointer in C/C++, we need to ensure we own the memory that pointer corresponds to. Just because a pointer holds an address does not mean we can safely read from or write to that location.
notes_text: The slide includes two images: movers carrying boxes (representing data to be stored) and the White House (representing an address you know but do not own). This analogy makes the abstract concept of memory ownership concrete and memorable for students.

images.description: Photo of movers carrying boxes, representing data that needs to be stored at a memory address
Photo of the White House at 1600 Pennsylvania Ave, illustrating the concept of knowing an address you do not own

title: Array / Pointer Relationship
summary: Explains that arrays guarantee owned memory with a valid address, while bare pointers may not point to valid or owned memory, risking segmentation faults.
main_text: Owning a home vs. writing a street address: A house is known by its address, and a house definitely has an address. But an address does not necessarily correspond to a house -- it may NOT correspond to a home, OR it could correspond to a home that you do NOT own. Arrays (owned memory) vs. pointers (addresses): An array (e.g., C-String like char name[6]) or other array definitely has a starting address (i.e., a char*). Having an array implies a VALID pointer (e.g., name). But a char* (pointer) MAY NOT necessarily correspond to a character array (C-String). Pointers DO NOT imply an underlying array or storage. So, care must be taken to ensure they point at good memory. Example: char name[6] = "Tommy"; creates owned memory at address 73d8. char* p1 = name; is valid because p1 points to owned memory. But char* p2; followed by p2[0] = 'a'; causes a Segmentation Fault because p2 does not point to any allocated memory.
notes_text: The diagram shows: name at 73d8 with 'Tommy\0', p1 holding 73d8 (valid), and p2 holding '????' (uninitialized, invalid). The house analogy reinforces the concept: just as a street address on paper does not guarantee a house exists there, a char* variable does not guarantee valid memory exists at the address it holds. A 'no entry' sign next to p2 emphasizes the danger.

images.description: Memory diagram showing char name[6] = 'Tommy' at address 73d8, char* p1 = name pointing to 73d8 (valid), and char* p2 with unknown address '????' causing a segmentation fault when dereferenced
Photo of row houses illustrating the analogy between houses (owned memory) and street addresses (pointers)

title: char* vs char Array - Common Error
summary: Demonstrates common errors when using strcpy with char* pointers that do not point to allocated memory, versus char arrays that own their storage.
main_text: Examine the code: char str1[40] = "hello world"; char* str2[40]; char* str3 = str2; char* str4;. The question is: will we be able to copy the strings using strcpy in each statement? strcpy(str2, str1); -- Does this work? Yes, because str2 is an array of 40 chars (owned memory). strcpy(str3, str1); -- Does this work? Yes, because str3 points to str2, which is an allocated array. strcpy(str4, str1); -- Does this work? No! str4 is an uninitialized char* pointer. It does not point to any allocated memory. You cannot just make up an address and go move into that apartment -- you must allocate/rent space first before you can go to an address and fill it in. Always ensure a char* POINTS at an array that you have allocated before you use the pointer.
notes_text: The memory diagram shows: str1 at address 73d0 as a large allocated array, str2 at address 7400 as another large allocated array, str3 pointing to str2's address (valid), and str4 holding '??' (uninitialized, invalid). This is one of the most common bugs students encounter: declaring a char* without pointing it at allocated memory and then trying to use it with strcpy or cin.

images.description: Memory diagram showing str1 as an allocated 40-byte array at 73d0, str2 as an allocated 40-byte array at 7400, str3 pointing to str2's address (valid), and str4 holding '??' (uninitialized, dangerous)

metadata.topic: char* vs char array common errors

title: C-Strings and char* Are Synonymous
summary: Establishes that char* should be mentally equated with C-String, but warns the pointer must actually reference a valid character array.
main_text: Moving forward, when you see type char* you should automatically think: C-String (i.e., a character array terminated with a null character). BUT, that char* must point to an ACTUAL character array. They should be synonymous in your head because 99% of the time, a char* will be used to point at a C-string. 1% of the time a char* will be pointing at a single character or array of characters that is not terminated with a null (which the documentation should describe). Many C/C++ library functions will ASSUME that a char* points at a C-string and treat it differently than other pointers (like int* or double*). cin/cout are the best example of this special treatment. Example: char name1[] = "Bill"; creates a char array, and name1 = 73d0 is a char* pointing to B, i, l, l, \0.
notes_text: The key mental model is: char* means C-string in practice. This helps students read function signatures and understand what is expected. However, the caveat is critical: the char* must actually point to valid, null-terminated memory. The 1% case (pointing to a single char or non-null-terminated array) is rare and should always be documented.

images.description: Memory diagram showing char name1[] = 'Bill' with name1 = 73d0 as a char* pointing to the character array containing B, i, l, l, \0

title: Expectations - cstring Library Functions Require NULL-Terminated Arrays
summary: Lists key cstring library functions and emphasizes that all expect the char* arguments to point to NULL-terminated character arrays.
main_text: All of the cstring library functions EXPECT that the char* you provide points to a NULL-terminated character array. The key functions listed are: int strlen(const char *dest) -- returns the length of the string. int strcmp(const char *str1, const char *str2) -- compares two strings. char *strcpy(char *dest, const char *src) -- copies src to dest. char *strcat(char *dest, const char *src) -- concatenates src onto dest. char *strchr(const char *str, char c) -- finds first occurrence of character c. All of these functions iterate through memory looking for the null terminator '\0'. If the char* does not point to a properly null-terminated array, these functions will read past the intended end of the string into arbitrary memory, causing undefined behavior.
notes_text: Notice the use of const char* for parameters that should not be modified (source strings, search targets) and plain char* for parameters that will be modified (destination buffers). This is a design pattern that communicates intent through the type system.

title: Converting C-Strings to Numeric Types - Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing atoi() and atof() functions for converting C-strings containing numeric characters into int and double values.
main_text: This section covers how to convert C-strings (character arrays containing digit characters) into numeric types like int and double. The functions atoi() and atof() from the <cstdlib> library provide this conversion capability. This is important when reading numeric input as text (e.g., from files or command-line arguments) and needing to perform arithmetic operations on the values.
notes_text: This topic connects to real-world programming scenarios where data arrives as text (CSV files, command-line arguments, network data) and must be converted to numeric types for computation.

title: Converting C-Strings to Numeric Types - Why Casting Fails
summary: Explains why you cannot simply cast a C-string to an int or double, because the cast converts the address rather than interpreting the digit characters.
main_text: How do we convert a C-string (char array) of digits to a number like an int or double? Can we just cast? No! Because the C-string is known by its address, casting (int) stri would just convert the pointer address to an integer, not interpret the digit characters. More importantly, we need to convert the many ASCII codes to a single number (e.g., the string "1889" consists of ASCII codes 49, 56, 56, 57 followed by 0 for '\0'). Casting gives us the address value (e.g., 0), not the number 1889. Example: char stri[5] = "1889"; int x = (int) stri; -- This gives x the address value, not 1889. The memory diagram shows stri at address 7320 containing ASCII values 49 ('1'), 56 ('8'), 56 ('8'), 57 ('9'), 0 ('\0'), and x receiving the value 0 (the cast pointer).
notes_text: This is a common misconception for beginners: thinking that (int) applied to a char* will somehow parse the string content. The cast actually reinterprets the pointer address as an integer. The ASCII value table in the diagram helps visualize that each character '1', '8', '8', '9' has its own numeric code (49, 56, 56, 57) that must be algorithmically combined to produce 1889.

images.description: Memory diagram showing char stri[5] at address 7320 containing ASCII values 49('1'), 56('8'), 56('8'), 57('9'), 0('\0'), and int x receiving value 0 from the failed cast

title: atoi() and atof() Functions
summary: Introduces atoi() and atof() from <cstdlib> for converting C-strings to int and double respectively, with code examples and memory diagrams.
main_text: To convert numeric C-Strings, we must use library functions. The <cstdlib> library provides functions that take char* (character string) inputs and convert to int or double types. atoi() or strtol() converts strings to ints (ASCII to Integer, and String to Long Int). atof() or strtod() converts strings to doubles (ASCII to float/double, and String to Double). strtol() and strtod() are newer and preferred over atoi() and atof() with extra features and error handling, but for simplicity, the course will likely just use atoi() and atof(). Example code: char stri[5] = "1889"; char strf[8] = "3.14159"; int x = atoi(stri); -- This is right! x gets value 1889. double y = atof(strd); -- This is right! y gets value 3.14159. The memory diagrams show stri at address 7320 with ASCII codes 49,56,56,57,0 being converted by atoi to integer 1889, and strf at address 7590 with ASCII codes 51,46,49,52,49,53,57,0 being converted by atof to double 3.14159.
notes_text: atoi stands for 'ASCII to integer' and atof stands for 'ASCII to float' (though it actually returns a double). These are older C library functions. The newer C++ alternatives strtol and strtod provide better error handling (they can tell you where parsing stopped and detect overflow), but atoi/atof are simpler to use for basic cases. Include <cstdlib> to use these functions.

images.description: Memory diagram showing stri at address 7320 with ASCII values 49,56,56,57,0 being converted via atoi() to integer 1889, and strf at address 7590 with ASCII values 51,46,49,52,49,53,57,0 being converted via atof() to double 3.14159

title: Backup - Array Memory Diagram for firstNeg (No Negatives)
summary: Backup reference diagram showing an integer array with no negative values, illustrating the case where firstNeg has no valid pointer to return.
main_text: This backup slide provides a standalone memory diagram showing an integer array dat with 5 elements at addresses 73a0 through 73b0. The values stored are: dat[0] = 14 at address 73a0, dat[1] = 8 at address 73a4, dat[2] = 3 at address 73a8 (highlighted in yellow/blue, indicating it was the location where a negative would have been found but the value is positive), dat[3] = 2 at address 73ac, dat[4] = 9 at address 73b0 (highlighted in yellow). The label 'int* return??' at the bottom indicates the function has no valid address to return since there are no negative numbers in the array. This reinforces the motivation for the NULL pointer.

It shows the case with array {14, 8, 3, 2, 9} where all values are positive, so the function cannot return a valid pointer. The highlighted cells (dat[2] with value 3 and dat[4] with value 9) draw attention to values that are positive rather than negative.

images.description: Memory diagram showing integer array dat with 5 elements (14, 8, 3, 2, 9) at addresses 73a0-73b0, with dat[2]=3 highlighted and 'int* return??' label indicating no valid return pointer exists
